title: Unstuffing & empty return
sceneDesc: At the consignee's warehouse, the cargo is unloaded from the container. The empty container is then trucked to an empty depot, inspected at the gate and prepared for its next trip.

1.tank: A hose empties my tank into the customer's storage. Then I need a special cleaning.
1.oog: A crane lifts {cargo} off me. Job done!
1.*: The customer's team unloads {cargo} — that's [[unstuffing]]. I'm empty again!

2.reefer: Unstuffing straight into the cold store: the cold chain must hold until the doors close behind the cargo. [TO VERIFY:v56]
2.tank: Discharge into the consignee's tanks; residues must be handled per DG rules before the tank is cleaned. [TO VERIFY:v59]
2.*: [[unstuffing|Unstuffing]] within the consignee's free time; any damage or shortage is documented with photos before the box leaves. [TO VERIFY:v70]

narration.3: Post-delivery: shortages and damage claims need notice within the applicable time limits; the box must be returned clean, emptied of dunnage and labels removed (DG placards too). [TO VERIFY:v71]

narration.1: A truck takes me, empty, to the depot chosen by the carrier.
narration.2: Empty return to the depot designated in the release; returning elsewhere can be refused or charged. [TO VERIFY:v71]
narration.3: Equipment control designates return depots by type and demand; empty repositioning is a major cost driven by trade imbalance. [TO VERIFY:v38]

narration.1: At the depot gate, someone checks me all around again and writes down my condition. My [[detention]] clock stops!
narration.2: Empty gate-in [[eir]]: condition and cleanliness recorded; import detention stops. Damage beyond normal wear is recharged per tariff. [TO VERIFY:v71] [TO VERIFY:v21]

3.reefer: Return EIR, wash and PTI before the next release; unit faults found at PTI may lead to recharges if caused by misuse. [TO VERIFY:v57] [TO VERIFY:v71]
3.tank: Tank cleaning at an approved station with a cleaning certificate before the next load. [TO VERIFY:v71]
3.*: Return EIR vs gate-out EIR decides damage recharges; M&R estimates follow repair standards. [TO VERIFY:v71]

narration.3: The consignee disputes a {cur}650 damage recharge for a dent recorded on the return EIR. The gate-out EIR at the import terminal says 'no damage', but its photos are blurry.

text.1: After this trip, I may carry an export from Europe — or travel back to Asia empty, because more goods go east to west than west to east. [TO VERIFY:v38]
text.2: Empty repositioning costs the industry billions each year; equipment control tries to reuse import boxes for exports ('street turns') wherever possible. [TO VERIFY:v38]

body.1: The customer unloads me at its own warehouse. If anything is damaged or missing, it takes photos and tells the carrier quickly.

body.2: Damage or shortage must be noted on delivery documents and notified within the time limits of the applicable rules; photos and survey reports are key. [TO VERIFY:v70]
body.3: Carrier liability depends on the B/L terms and the applicable regime (e.g. Hague-Visby); the SLAC clause shifts packing issues to the shipper. [TO VERIFY:v50]

body.1: The carrier chooses where I'm returned, so I can be cleaned, repaired and used again.
body.2: Designated by the carrier per type and location; returning to another depot may be refused or charged. [TO VERIFY:v71]

reefer.1: Reefers are washed and their cooling machine tested before the next trip.
reefer.2: Washing and PTI before the next release; damage to the unit is checked. [TO VERIFY:v57]

tank.1: My tank is cleaned and a certificate proves it's ready for the next product.
tank.2: Cleaning at an approved station with a cleaning certificate; residues of dangerous goods are handled under DG rules. [TO VERIFY:v59] [TO VERIFY:v71]

body.1: My condition report at return. If I'm damaged and the earlier report said I was fine, the customer may have to pay for the repair.
The clock stops when I'm back at the depot. If I came back late, the customer pays detention for the extra days.
body.2: Import detention ends at empty gate-in at the designated depot. Illustrative: {freeDays} free days, then {cur}80/day. [TO VERIFY:v21] [TO VERIFY:v12]

1.2: Compared with the full gate-out EIR at the import terminal: damage that appeared in between is recharged per tariff. [TO VERIFY:v71]

2.2: Dirty boxes, leftover dunnage or old DG labels trigger cleaning fees. [TO VERIFY:v71]

3.2: Empty gate-in time stops import detention. [TO VERIFY:v21]

2.prompt: What decides whether the consignee pays for the dent?

options.text: Comparing this return EIR with the gate-out EIR at the import terminal

options.fb: Equipment damage follows the interchange terms, not the Incoterm.

2.explain: Two EIRs bracket the custody period; damage recorded between them is recharged per the carrier's equipment terms. [TO VERIFY:v71]

3.prompt: The box was returned to a different depot, 30 km closer to the consignee. Likely outcome?

options.text: Refused, or accepted with a wrong-depot / repositioning charge; detention may run until it reaches an accepted depot
Accepted with no consequence: all depots are the same
options.fb: Depots are contracted and stocked per carrier needs.

options.text: The carrier pays the extra trip
options.fb: The return location was part of the release terms.
It's an equipment issue, not a customs one.

3.explain: Return locations reflect equipment control's plan; deviations cost money. [TO VERIFY:v71]

documents: **Return EIR** — condition and time at empty gate-in. [TO VERIFY:v71]
**Damage report / M&R estimate** if repairs are needed.
**Detention invoice** — if free time was exceeded. [TO VERIFY:v21]
costs: **Damage recharge** per tariff and repair standards. [TO VERIFY:v71]
risks: **Leftover DG labels or residues** → refusal or fees. [TO VERIFY:v59]
**Box left idle** → equipment shortage elsewhere. [TO VERIFY:v38]
jobs: **Equipment control** — return depots, repositioning, street turns. [TO VERIFY:v38]
**D&D team** — detention and damage invoicing, disputes. [TO VERIFY:v72]

incoNote.DPU: Under DPU, the seller unloads the goods: risk and cost pass to the buyer once they are unloaded here.
incoNote.*: Empty return and detention follow the contract of carriage and the sales contract, not the Incoterm.

1: The customer unloads me and reports any damage quickly.
I go back empty to a depot chosen by the carrier, where my condition is checked.
My detention clock stops when I'm back — then I'm ready for a new journey.
2: Unstuffing within free time; claims need documented evidence.
Return to the designated depot; EIRs decide damage recharges.
Equipment control reuses or repositions the empty — trade imbalance makes this costly.
3: D&D and damage disputes are won or lost on evidence (EIRs, photos, timestamps).
Bill per tariff consistently; waivers are documented commercial decisions.
Street turns and smart return depots cut empty repositioning.

1.prompt: I'm empty and clean at the depot. What happens next?
1.hint: Containers are made to travel again and again.

options.text: I'm used for a new booking — maybe an export from Europe — or sent back empty where boxes are needed.
options.confirm: Yes! Equipment control gives me a new job. My journey starts again with a booking. Congratulations — you've followed me all the way!

options.text: I'm scrapped: containers are used only once.
options.why: Containers are built to last many years and many trips.
options.realLife: A box typically serves for well over a decade.
options.whenRight: Only when it's too damaged or old to repair.

options.text: I stay at the depot until my first shipper books again.
options.why: Any customer can use me; equipment control decides.
options.realLife: Idle boxes cost money and create shortages elsewhere.

2.prompt: Empty returned and inspected at the depot. What happens next?

options.text: Equipment control allocates the box: a new export booking from the region, or empty repositioning to a deficit area.
options.confirm: Correct. Reusing import boxes for exports avoids empty moves; the rest are repositioned where demand is. The journey loops back to step 1. [TO VERIFY:v38]

options.text: The consignee now owns the box.
options.realLife: Keeping it would mean detention, then a lost-box claim.

options.text: The importer must return it to the origin terminal in Asia.
options.why: The consignee's obligation ends at the designated return depot.

options.text: It waits for the original shipper to book again.
options.why: Containers are pooled and reused by any customer.

3.prompt: Case: {cur}650 damage recharge disputed; gate-out EIR says 'no damage' but its photos are blurry. What is the right approach?

options.text: Review both EIRs, photos and the M&R estimate; if the evidence that the damage occurred in the consignee's custody is weak, adjust or waive — and fix the photo process at the terminal.
options.confirm: Right. Recharges need evidence: two EIRs with usable photos and an approved repair estimate. Weak evidence loses disputes and customers; process fixes prevent repeats. [TO VERIFY:v71] [TO VERIFY:v72]

options.text: Insist on payment: the return EIR shows the dent.
options.why: The return EIR alone doesn't prove when the damage happened.
options.realLife: Disputes escalate; regulators or courts may side with the customer.
options.whenRight: When both EIRs clearly support it.

options.text: Waive automatically to keep the customer happy.
options.why: Automatic waivers ignore valid recharges and set precedents.
options.whenRight: When the evidence is genuinely insufficient — after review.

options.why: The contractual counterparty for the recharge is the merchant who held the box.
options.realLife: The merchant may recover from its haulier, but that's their relationship.
options.whenRight: Under carrier haulage, the carrier may recover from its own subcontractor.
